about: The wording rules scripts/bias_check.py applies to every candidate-facing text. Each rule names its class, its severity, the kinds of text it applies to, why it matters and what to say instead. 'guards' are sentence-level patterns that switch the rule off for that sentence; 'text_guards' switch it off for the whole text (a driving job may lawfully ask for a licence). Patterns are lower-case regular expressions, matched in English only. A rule that does not match is not a clearance.
eeo_guard: (equal (employment )?opportunity|\beeo\b|\beoe\b|without regard to|regardless of|(does|do) not discriminate|all qualified applicants|reasonable accommodation|affirmative action|we welcome applicants|protected (veteran|characteristic|status)|(will )?never ask (you )?(about|for)|we do not ask|we don't ask)
driving_job: \b(drivers?\b(?!'s licen|s' licen| licen)|driving (job|role|position)|delivery (driver|associate|route)|deliver(ing)? (packages|orders|groceries|food)|courier|route (driver|sales)|cdl|forklift operator|drive (your|a|the) (own )?(car|vehicle|van|truck|company vehicle)|rideshare|mileage reimbursement|van route)\b
physical_demands: (\b\d+\s*(lbs?|pounds|kg|kilos)\b|on your feet|standing (for|up to)|stand for|walk(ing)? (up to )?\d|\b\d+[- ]hour shifts? on|bend(ing)?,|bending|kneel|climb(ing)? (ladders|stairs)|repetitive|temperatures?|freezer|cooler|cold environment|\bheat\b|outdoors in|noise|loud)

rules.why: A job title with a gender in it tells half the people reading it that the job is not for them, and in hourly hiring that shows up as fewer applications, not complaints.
rules.instead: Use the neutral title: sales associate, server, host, handyperson, supervisor, crew, staff, porter.

rules.why: Writing about the hire as 'he' assumes who the hire is.
rules.instead: Address the reader: 'you will', 'your shift'.

rules.why: Masculine-coded and hype words narrow who sees themselves in the job, and describe nothing about the shift.
rules.instead: Say what the work is: 'you'll restock 20 aisles a night' tells people more than any label.

rules.why: Personality words with a gender attached narrow the pool and describe nothing you can check.
rules.instead: Name the behaviour: 'greets every customer within 10 seconds'.

patterns: \b(culture fit|cultural fit|fit in with (our|the) (team|crew|culture)|one of the (guys|boys|girls))\b
rules.why: 'Fit' is where a decision gets made on similarity rather than the job, and written down it reads as a reason.
rules.instead: Name the job requirement the person did or did not meet.

patterns: \b(no older than|not older than|under the age of|maximum age|max\.? age|between the ages of|aged between)\b
\b(no more than|not more than|maximum( of)?|max\.?|up to) \d+ years?'?( of)? (experience|exp\b)
rules.why: Wording that prefers younger applicants, or caps experience, deters people 40 and over, a protected group under federal law.
rules.instead: State what the job needs. A minimum age the law requires ('must be 18 or older') is fine.

rules.why: Age-coded the other way: it narrows the pool and says nothing about the job.
rules.instead: Name the behaviour you want.

rules.why: Asking for age, a birth year or a graduation year before a decision invites age discrimination claims and tells you nothing about the job.
rules.instead: If the role has a legal minimum age, ask 'Are you 18 or older?' and nothing more.

rules.why: Citizenship and origin questions route into national-origin and citizenship discrimination. What you may ask is whether the person is authorised to work.
rules.instead: Ask: 'Are you legally authorised to work in the United States?' Verify documents only after hire, through Form I-9.

rules.why: 'Native speaker' and 'no accent' are national-origin proxies. A language requirement is fine when the job needs it; the origin is not.
rules.instead: Describe the task: 'can follow spoken safety instructions and read a pick list in English'.

rules.why: Health and disability questions before an offer are restricted under the ADA, and fitness wording deters disabled applicants who could do the job, with or without an accommodation.
rules.instead: State the task and how often: 'lift cases of up to 40 lbs, about 50 times a shift'. Ask 'Can you do this, with or without a reasonable accommodation?'

patterns: \b(children|kids|child ?care|babysitter|daycare|pregnan\w*|expecting a baby|married|marital status|maiden name|spouse|husband|wife|boyfriend|girlfriend|family plans|start(ing)? a family|plan(ning)? (to have|on having) (kids|children|a baby))\b
rules.why: Questions about children, pregnancy or marriage are used as availability screens and are evidence of sex discrimination when someone is turned down.
rules.instead: Ask everyone the same thing: 'Can you work the posted schedule, nights and weekends included?'

rules.why: A requirement about family is a screen on sex and caring responsibilities.
rules.instead: State the schedule and let people judge it.

rules.why: Questions about religion invite discrimination claims. Days someone cannot work are an accommodation conversation, not a screening question.
rules.instead: Ask which days and times they can work, the same way for everyone.

rules.why: A sex preference in a job ad or screen is unlawful outside a narrow bona fide occupational qualification.
rules.instead: State the requirement of the job itself.

rules.why: Height and weight rules screen out women and some national-origin groups at higher rates, and are rarely what the job needs.
rules.instead: State the task: what has to be reached or lifted, and how often.

rules.why: An arrest is not a conviction. Screening on arrests has a disparate impact by race and is not job-related.
rules.instead: Leave it out. If a conviction check is needed, run it after a conditional offer, and assess it against the job.

rules.why: Many states and cities bar criminal-history questions on the application or before a conditional offer, and blanket exclusions have a disparate impact by race.
rules.instead: Move it after the conditional offer, and assess the offence, the time since and the job. Check your state and city rules.

rules.why: A growing number of states and cities ban asking for pay history, because it carries past pay gaps into the next job.
rules.instead: State the pay for the role, and ask whether it works for them.

rules.why: Car ownership tracks income, age and disability. You probably mean 'can get here for a 5am start', which people on a bus route can do every day.
rules.instead: Say the start time and the location: 'Shifts start at 5am at our Dayton store (bus route 17 stops outside).'

rules.why: A licence asked for on a job with no driving filters out people who do not drive, often for reasons of income or disability, and is sometimes a stand-in for an ID.
rules.instead: If the job does not involve driving, drop it. If you mean an ID, say 'a government-issued photo ID'.

rules.why: 'Flexible' is unfalsifiable at application, filters out carers and students, and is a known reason people quit in week two when the real pattern arrives.
rules.instead: Publish the actual pattern: 'a rotating schedule, four shifts a week, posted two weeks ahead, including one weekend day'.

rules.why: An open 'any restrictions?' invites answers about childcare, religion, health and appointments, and files them in your records.
rules.instead: Ask which blocks they can work, as checkboxes: weekday mornings, weekday evenings, nights, Saturdays, Sundays.

rules.why: Appearance standards route into race (hair) and religion (beards, head coverings) unless they are written as a specific, job-related standard with alternatives.
rules.instead: Write the standard: 'uniform provided; hair tied back or covered in food areas; respirator users need a seal, and we'll discuss alternatives'.

rules.why: Gaps stand in for health, disability, caring, pregnancy and criminal record. Screening on them excludes all of those at once.
rules.instead: Ask about recent experience of the work itself, if you need it at all.

rules.why: Most of your strongest applicants are working a notice period.
rules.instead: Give the real window: 'start within two weeks'.

guards: \b(no experience|experience not required|not required|we train|we'll train|paid training|a plus|preferred|nice to have)\b
rules.why: Years of experience on a role you train in days is the most common needless filter in frontline hiring.
rules.instead: Ask what happens if you hire someone without it. If the answer is 'we train them', move it to 'nice to have' or drop it.

rules.why: An open 'about you' surfaces protected characteristics and gets scored on fluency, which is rarely the job.
rules.instead: Ask about a specific situation the job contains.
